entities.summary:
Henry III von Virneburg was a pivotal figure in the ecclesiastical and political landscape of Medieval Europe. As Archbishop and Elector of Mainz from 1328/37 to 1346/53, he played a crucial role in shaping the religious and political fortunes of the Holy Roman Empire. His tenure was marked by significant events, including the appointment of Pope John XXII, the rise of the Hussite movement, and the ongoing struggle for power between the papacy and the Holy Roman Emperor. Despite facing numerous challenges, Henry III von Virneburg remained a steadfast advocate for the authority of the Catholic Church and the traditions of the Holy Roman Empire. His legacy continued to influence the development of European politics and religion for centuries to come.

Henry III von Virneburg was born into a noble family in the 13th century and received a traditional education in law, philosophy, and theology. He entered the service of the Archbishop of Mainz at a young age and quickly rose through the ranks to become a trusted advisor and confidant to the Archbishop. When the Archbishop died in 1328, Henry III von Virneburg was elected as his successor, becoming one of the most powerful men in Germany.

As Archbishop, Henry III von Virneburg oversaw the construction of numerous churches, monasteries, and other ecclesiastical buildings, many of which still stand today. He also played a key role in the development of the Mainz University, which became a center of learning and intellectual inquiry in the region. Despite his many accomplishments, Henry III von Virneburg's life was cut short when he died on December 29, 1353, at the age of approximately 65.
